title: Managed Services Organizations vs. Alternative Business Structures: Two models for outside investment in law firms
author: David Horniak · Merrick Doll · Neil K. Vohra · Corey Mirman

dom.t: Outside capital: Permission does not create investable firms

st.t: Ownership reform: Investment openings may miss justice needs
st.an: The source shifts the inquiry from whether ownership reform reduces the justice gap to which investment structure—direct ABS ownership or an MSO—best suits firms and investors. It materially explains the two routes and jurisdictional constraints, while offering little evidence about actual access or consumer outcomes and treating Arizona’s growing ABS count as success.
qs: In this article, we break down these two models and explain why, for many law firms and investors, the MSO model may be the more attractive option.

In Utah, to obtain regulatory approval to become an ABS Law Firm, the firm must demonstrate that outside investment "will allow it to reach Utah consumers currently underserved by the legal market" and that "the impact on Utah consumers [will] be substantial relative to the entity's overall reach." Utah Supreme Court, Letter to Utah Legal Services Innovation Committee, Sep.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source does not assess AI’s jagged task-level capabilities, selective deployment, verification, user expertise, or AI-driven work redesign. It instead examines MSOs as an investment and shared-services structure relative to ABS law firms. Its claims about scalable resource pooling are tangentially relevant to operating models, but do not establish a position on the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: Additionally, because the MSO operates as a vendor, it can be scaled independently from the law firm(s) from whence it came.

This sort of resource-pooling can confer benefits on law firms in the form of economies of scale, improved technology and tools, and greater staff specialization and professionalization than certain law firms might be able to facilitate on their own.

st.t: Outside capital: Permission does not create investable firms
st.an: The source accepts that regulatory permission alone does not solve the investment problem and materially develops the synthesis by distinguishing ABS ownership from the more geographically flexible MSO model, specifying substantive separation safeguards, and acknowledging that investor-compensation constraints leave neither structure universally adequate.
qs: ## Conclusion  Currently, neither the ABS Law Firm model nor the MSO model is a perfect solution to the challenge of facilitating nonlawyer ownership of law firms.

st.t: Workflow unbundling: Buyers challenge time-based production
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s claim that scaling technology-enabled legal delivery depends on capital and governance, and materially develops it by identifying private capital as an alternative to debt while explaining how Rule 5.4-style ownership and fee-sharing restrictions constrain investment structures.
qs: For professional practices looking to scale, adopt new technologies, or make other investments in their business, private capital can be an alternative to traditional debt financing.
This is, in significant part, attributable to a longstanding patchwork of state laws and rules that prohibit nonlawyer fee-sharing and ownership of law firms, as embodied in ABA Model Rule 5.4.

kp.k: Ownership restrictions constrain private capital for law firm investment
kp.d: The authors argue that private capital can finance professional practices' expansion and technology adoption, but US law firms have attracted less outside investment than medical, dental, veterinary and accounting practices because most jurisdictions prohibit nonlawyer ownership and fee-sharing. They describe professional practices as generally predictable, linearly scalable investments, while noting that contingency-fee law firms can be exceptions. The article addresses investment structures rather than specific AI applications or measured AI effects.
qs: For professional practices looking to scale, adopt new technologies, or make other investments in their business, private capital can be an alternative to traditional debt financing.
This is, in significant part, attributable to a longstanding patchwork of state laws and rules that prohibit nonlawyer fee-sharing and ownership of law firms, as embodied in ABA Model Rule 5.4.
They are also scalable, albeit on a linear basis.

kp.k: ABS permits direct ownership, profit participation and strategic influence
kp.d: The authors describe the ideal ABS law firm as enabling nonlawyer equity ownership, direct participation in legal fees and macro-level business management, while protecting lawyers' professional judgment in individual matters. Arizona's model combines direct equity investment with integrated business leadership and legal operations under regulatory oversight.
qs: The ABS Law Firm model, at least in its platonic ideal form, is true nonlawyer investment in, and ownership of, law firms.

It permits private investors to share directly in fees earned by the firm and gives them a voice in the management of and direction of the firm's business on a macro level, without impinging on lawyers' professional judgment or ethical obligations in individual cases.
Integrated control and alignment between business leadership and legal operations within a single entity, subject to robust regulatory oversight

kp.k: Jurisdictional differences sharply limit available ABS investment routes
kp.d: The authors distinguish Arizona and Puerto Rico from Washington, DC and Utah. DC permits ownership by individuals providing supporting professional services, not passive investors. They report that Utah's September 5, 2024 approval conditions require substantial impact on underserved Utah consumers, which they interpret as excluding most firms. Puerto Rico caps nonlawyer ownership at 49 percent and limits investors to supplying capital. They characterize Arizona ABS firms as successful without presenting quantitative evidence and say Puerto Rico's outcomes remain uncertain.
qs: This restriction "does not permit an individual or entity to acquire all or any part of the ownership of a law partnership or other form of law practice organization for investment or other purposes."

the firm must demonstrate that outside investment "will allow it to reach Utah consumers currently underserved by the legal market" and that "the impact on Utah consumers [will] be substantial relative to the entity's overall reach."
It prohibits nonlawyer owners from acquiring more than 49 percent of a law firm, and it prohibits nonlawyer investors from providing any services other than investment dollars to the law firm.
By all accounts, ABS Law Firms in Arizona are finding success, with new ABS Law Firms emerging on a regular basis. It's too early to say whether the same will be true in Puerto Rico.

kp.k: MSOs separate investable infrastructure from lawyer-owned legal practice
kp.d: Under the two-company MSO model, outside investment goes into nonlegal operations rather than ownership of the law firm. The lawyer-owned core practices law, controls professional judgment and receives legal fees. A separately owned MSO supplies operational services, including technology, marketing, staffing, finance and accounting, and owns or licenses critical intellectual property such as software and the firm's trade name. Its compensation takes the form of service fees rather than ownership participation in legal fees.
qs: Rather, it carves out the nonlegal parts of a law firm and channels outside investment into those parts only.
One entity, the "core" law firm, continues to be owned entirely by lawyers and exclusively practices law and receives legal fees.

Another entity, the MSO, is owned by investors, entrepreneurs, or others (lawyers or nonlawyers), and absorbs essentially all of the nonlegal business infrastructure previously handled by the law firm.
Owns and licenses to the law firm critical intellectual property, including software and the trade name under which the firm practices

kp.k: MSO compliance requires independent judgment and genuine operational separation
kp.d: The authors identify the services agreement and its actual operation as central to ethical compliance. They prescribe reasonable market-based compensation untied to legal fees, revenues or profits; no MSO contractual control over legal judgment, client selection, case strategy or settlements; and separate governance, financials and personnel structures. These are presented as conditions for a compliant structure, not evidence that every MSO satisfies professional rules.
qs: The key to ethical compliance is the services agreement between the law firm and the MSO.

**Avoids fee-sharing** by ensuring the MSO's compensation is not tied to the law firm's fees, revenues, or profits, but is instead a "reasonable" market price for the services delivered – akin to any other third-party vendor arrangement
**Preserves lawyer independence** by giving the MSO no contractual right to control legal judgment, client selection, case strategy, or settlement decisions
**Maintains real corporate and operational separation** between the law firm and the MSO, with distinct governance, financials, and personnel structures

kp.k: MSO platforms consolidate infrastructure without merging legal entities
kp.d: The authors report that legal-market MSOs increasingly acquire or build infrastructure serving multiple firms while leaving the legal entities separate. They explicitly analogize this arrangement to established management-company structures in medicine, dentistry and veterinary practice that navigate ownership and fee-sharing restrictions.
qs: In practice, MSOs in the legal market increasingly act as platforms that "collect" law firms, acquiring or building the back-office infrastructure of multiple firms without merging their legal entities.

This is directly analogous to long-established models in medicine, dentistry, and veterinary practices, where management companies or MSOs sit alongside professional entities to navigate corporate-practice-of-medicine and fee-sharing restrictions.

kp.k: Interstate professional rules restrict ABS expansion and referral strategies
kp.d: Citing ABA Formal Opinion 91-360, the authors state that lawful nonlawyer ownership in one jurisdiction does not permit branch offices or firm operations in jurisdictions prohibiting that ownership. They describe referral-based workarounds as practically difficult and increasingly restricted. They quote California AB 931's prohibition on direct or indirect fee-sharing with out-of-state ABSs, subject to an exception for attorneys also licensed in the approving state and paid for legal services there; their broader characterization is that the statute effectively forecloses financial relationships with California firms.
qs: ABA Formal Opinion 91-360 provides that a nonlawyer-owned firm lawfully organized in one jurisdiction cannot maintain a "branch office" or otherwise operate as a firm in jurisdictions that prohibit nonlawyer ownership.
But these strategies face significant practical challenges, and some jurisdictions are actively taking steps to foreclose them.

California's legislature recently passed AB 931, which provides that "[n]o attorney licensed or otherwise authorized to practice in [California] shall share legal fees directly or indirectly with an out-of-state alternative business structure[,] unless" the attorney is also licensed in the state where the ABS Law Firm is approved and the fees are compensation for the provision of legal services *in that state*.

kp.k: MSO geographic flexibility potentially improves scale and technology access
kp.d: The authors argue that retaining a traditional lawyer-owned firm without fee-sharing makes the MSO model more geographically flexible than ABS ownership. They suggest an MSO can independently serve firms across states, producing economies of scale, better technology and greater staff specialization. They also predict that adding service relationships may allow faster growth than expanding a firm's lawyer headcount or client base; these benefits are possibilities rather than quantified findings.
qs: Because the core law firm in the MSO model remains a traditional, lawyer-owned professional entity that does not share its fees with the MSO, it is widely understood not to run afoul of Rule 5.4(d)
It can grow to serve multiple law firms across multiple states – just as outsourced IT providers, e-discovery vendors, and staffing companies already do today.

This sort of resource-pooling can confer benefits on law firms in the form of economies of scale, improved technology and tools, and greater staff specialization and professionalization than certain law firms might be able to facilitate on their own.

An MSO may also be able to grow in size – by entering into service relationships with additional law firms – faster than a traditional law firm (or an ABS Law Firm) can grow its size by increasing lawyer head count and/or attracting new clients.

kp.k: Investor upside remains MSOs' central unresolved tradeoff
kp.d: The authors favor MSOs for many investors under current geographic restrictions but acknowledge that prohibitions on fee-sharing make participation in the core firm's profitability difficult and can favor ABS ownership in some circumstances. They state that bespoke MSO fee arrangements have been implemented without providing examples or a universal solution. Their recommendation is conditional: MSOs may remain the preferred investment structure until ABS authorization expands.
qs: The main challenge of the MSO model is enabling investors to benefit from the core law firm's profitability without violating fee-sharing rules.
This limitation may in some situations make the ABS Law Firm model more suitable.
However, while there is currently no clear "one-size-fits-all" solution to this problem, bespoke fee arrangements for MSOs can be (and have been) implemented).
Unless and until the ABS Law Firm model is adopted in more jurisdictions, the MSO model may be the structure of choice for nonlawyers to invest in law firm businesses.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The source makes no explicit claims or predictions about AI changing legal services.
pts.d: David Horniak, Merrick Doll, Neil K. Vohra and Corey Mirman compare ABS and MSO structures for outside investment in US law firm businesses. They claim that private capital can support technology adoption and that MSO resource-pooling can improve technology and tools, but they do not identify AI or attribute any changes to it. This is a legal-market source, not a cross-domain source; its investment and regulatory claims should not be recast as AI predictions.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.d: The article's supporting material concerns regulatory authority, investment structures and analogies with MSOs in other professional practices. It includes jurisdiction-specific rules, ABA Formal Opinion 91-360, a Utah Supreme Court letter and California AB 931. It supplies no AI adoption data, performance benchmarks, deployment cases or measured effects on legal work.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: No AI-related timeframe or conditions are stated.
pts.d: The authors' conditional outlook concerns the regulatory availability of ABS structures, not AI development or adoption. Their preference for MSOs is qualified by whether more jurisdictions permit ABS law firms.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: No population is identified as affected specifically by AI.
pts.d: The article discusses US law firms, nonlawyer investors and MSO operators as participants affected by investment and ownership structures. Potential benefits for firms include shared infrastructure, improved tools and staff specialization, but the authors do not link these benefits to AI or predict AI-related changes in staffing, client outcomes or access to justice.
